amendments.rule: **A verb the ASV renders as a light verb plus a complement heads on the complement, not on the light verb.** This is rule 31's test applied to a verb: drop each word in turn, and the head is the one whose loss loses the lexeme. `הַאֲזִין` → *Give ear unto* heads on *ear*, because *give* alone gives anything; so too `הִשְׁתַּחֲוָה` → *did obeisance*, `נוֹעַץ` → *took counsel*, `הִמְלִיךְ` → *make king*, `הוֹדָה` → *give thanks*, `כִּלָּה` → *made an end*, `עוּד` → *bear witness*, `חָנַן` → *make supplication*, `בּוֹשׁ` → *put to shame*. The complement need not be a noun: an adjective (`הִכְבִּיד` → *made heavy*, `גָּדַל` → *make greater*) and a second verb (`חָטָא` hiphil → *made to sin*, `אָכַל` → *did eat*) are read the same way. Rule 24's *lexical predicate over subjects and auxiliaries* is about `was gathered`, and must not be read as a preference for the English verb — that reasoning would head *make king* on *make*. **A phrasal particle is not a complement.** `שָׁלַח` → *put forth*, `סוּר` → *take away*, and `נָתַן` → *put away* are one lexical verb plus its particle, and the head stays on the verb; the same subtraction says so, since *forth* and *away* alone name nothing. **A supplied object is not a complement either, and that holds of any verb's rendering and not only a light verb's.** Where the ASV writes an object pronoun inside or beside a Hebrew verb's rendering — `וַיַּפֵּל` → *he let* ***it*** *fall*, `וַיַּשְׁקְ` → *gave* ***them*** *drink*, `אֲנִי שָׁמָעְתִּי` → *I have heard* ***it*** — read whether an object morpheme is present. Where one is, it takes the pronoun under rule 18 and the verb keeps the rest, as in `וַיַּעֲבִירֵם` → *caused* ***them*** *to pass through*. Where none is, the pronoun answers to no morpheme, is its own `added` unit under rule 30, and does not join the verb merely because it stands inside or beside its rendering; rule 17's permission reaches a pronoun realizing the verb's own person and number, which is a subject, and never an object the Hebrew does not write, exactly as that rule leaves a supplied lexical subject noun `added`. The verb's unit is discontinuous around such a pronoun under rule 25. **This applies only to a pronoun that truly supplies an object.** A reflexive pronoun the ASV uses to render the Hebrew verb's own voice or its elative sense is part of that verb's unit, because the source verb licenses it: `אִכַּף` → *bow myself* keeps *myself* with the Niphal verb and heads on *bow*, and `הִגְדִּיל עַל` → *magnified yourselves against* keeps *yourselves* with the Hiphil on the same ground. Position inside the English verb phrase is not what makes a word part of the verb's rendering — the complement, or the source verb's own voice or sense, must license it, and an unsupported object does not. **A supplied object noun is read on those same terms, and what decides it is whether the English noun writes the verb's own lexeme.** Where the ASV completes a Hebrew verb with an object noun the Hebrew does not write, run rule 31's subtraction on that noun. Where it does not carry the verb's lexeme, it answers to no morpheme, is its own `added` unit under rule 30, and does not join the verb merely because it stands inside its rendering: `לֹא שָׁאָלוּ` → *asked* ***counsel*** *not* leaves *counsel* `added`, because `שָׁאַל` is the asking and *asked* has already written it, exactly as rule 17 leaves a supplied lexical subject noun `added` and rule 20 a supplied lexical verb. Where it does carry the lexeme, the noun is part of that verb's one rendering, joins its unit, and the head goes by the same subtraction to whichever word carries the lexeme: `וַיַּעֲשׂוּ` → *did work* is one unit on the verb, headed on *did*, because `עָשָׂה` is the doing and the working alike and neither English word is a complement the other lacks. Read the source verb's lexeme rather than the English phrase's shape, since this rule's light-verb clause governs where the supplied noun is what carries that lexeme — `נוֹעַץ` → *took counsel* heads on *counsel* — and this sentence governs where the verb's own English word has written it already. A supplied possessive standing on such a noun is disposed of by rule 18's closing sentence and is not made the verb's by the noun beside it. **But a preposition the ASV supplies to reach the verb's own object is part of that rendering.** Where the Hebrew writes a bare direct object — no object marker on it and no preposition of its own — and the English verb reaches that object through a preposition the ASV has written, the preposition belongs to the verb's unit and not to the object noun's: `חָמְסוּ תוֹרָתִי` → *have done violence* ***to*** *my law*, `תְּבַצְּעִי רֵעַיִךְ` → *hast greedily gained* ***of*** *thy neighbors*, `הֵקַלּוּ אָב וָאֵם` → *have set light* ***by*** *father and mother*, `אֲבַקֵּשׁ אִישׁ` → *sought* ***for*** *a man*, `טָחוּ תָּפֵל` → *have daubed ... with untempered mortar*. This is rule 16's reasoning where no marker stands to take the word: the same subtraction test finds that dropping it diminishes nothing but the object relation, and the object noun's own English is the noun. The unit is discontinuous under rule 25 where other material stands between the verb and the preposition, and the head is unaffected — it stays on the lexical verb, or on the complement where this rule's light-verb clause puts it. **And the object so reached may be a pronominal suffix on the verb rather than a noun.** Where a verbal object suffix stands with no preposition of its own and the English rendering reaches it through a supplied preposition — `יִבְּמָהּ` → *perform the duty of a husband's brother* ***unto*** *her*, `יַבְּמִי` → *perform the duty of a husband's brother* ***unto*** *me* — that preposition belongs to the verb's unit on exactly the terms just given, and the suffix keeps only the pronoun rule 18 writes for it. Do not read rule 18's *the English pronoun that realizes it* as reaching the preposition standing beside that pronoun: what that rule places is the pronoun, and a preposition the English verb's valency licenses is the verb's whether its object is a noun or a suffix. Rule 40 does not reach such a suffix either, since no preposition morpheme stands in the clause for the recasting to silence. Test by subtraction as before — drop the English preposition and ask whether anything but the object relation is diminished. Two limits. Where an object marker or a preposition of the object's own is present, that morpheme takes the word under rules 16 and 11, a present morpheme taking its English before a supplied reading does. And this does not touch rule 33: a function word supplied for an adverbial accusative is licensed by that noun's own case-function and stays with the noun, whereas a word supplied for a direct object is licensed by the English verb's valency, so read which the Hebrew noun is before placing it.
amendments.why: Rule 44 already ruled that a supplied object is not a complement, but stated and reasoned that clause for object pronouns only, leaving a supplied object noun to be decided by analogy every time. JOS.9 met the case twice in opposite directions in the same chapter and the difference is invisible to the cross-verse table, because an `added` unit has no source token: 9.14 marks the supplied counsel `added` beside sha'al, while 9.4 keeps work inside asah's unit in did work. The deciding fact is whether the English noun writes the verb's own lexeme, which is rule 31's subtraction already cited in this rule, and the qualification belongs here rather than as a new rule pointing back, since the existing sentence about pronouns would otherwise read as though it settled the noun case too. Returned as an amendment with the whole of rule 44 quoted back, including the phrasal-particle, reflexive, supplied-preposition, suffix and two-limits paragraphs, which are unchanged.

conventions: The Gibeonite deception is narrated in 9.4-5 and then repeated in the envoys' own words in 9.12-13, and the two tellings do not write the same Hebrew, so an apparent split between them must be checked against the source before it is treated as one. The clause yabesh ... haya niqqudim is asyndetic in 9.5, where the ASV's second 'and' is `added` under rule 14, and writes a waw in 9.12, where that waw takes the same word; the participles of 9.5 (bal, metulla'ot) become a finite balu in 9.13, so the copulas fall differently. Read the two speeches against each other rather than assuming the chapter has one practice.

report: Read all 51 candidate groups. None holds one construction analysed two ways with nothing in the source to license the difference: every multi-treatment bucket is the ASV's own choice of connective (waw to and/but/then/so/therefore/Now/that/when/both), of preposition (lamed to to/unto/with/for), or of determiner, each read off the English as rules 14 and 11 direct.

The candidate table is blind to `added`, so the dump was read end to end for supplied English. Four `added` units - thereof (9.1), and (9.5), our (9.12), counsel (9.14) - plus one supplied word folded into its verb, work in 9.4's 'did work'. The line between them is whether the supplied English word writes the source verb's own lexeme: asah is the doing and the working alike, sha'al is the asking and not the counsel, and thereof and our answer to no morpheme at all. Both sides are right, so no patch; but rule 44 stated the supplied-object case for pronouns only, and the amendment below closes that gap rather than leaving it for the next chapter.

9.5 against 9.12: the same clause (yabesh ... haya niqqudim) is asyndetic in the narrator's telling and writes a waw in the envoys' telling, so the `added` and of 9.5 and the aligned waw of 9.12 are both correct. This is the chapter's one place where two near-identical verses could be mistaken for a split, and it is recorded as a convention.

Preposition plus construct noun: fused at 9.1 and 9.10 (be-'ever to 'beyond'), 9.7, 9.16 and 9.22 (be-qereb to 'among'), 9.16 (acharei asher to 'after'), 9.21 (ka'asher to 'as'), 9.22 (lammah to 'Wherefore'), 9.24 (mippene to 'because of') and 9.25 as corrected (be-'ene to 'unto'); split at 9.24's first mippenekhem ('from before') and at 9.25's be-yadekha ('in thy hand'). Every case follows rule 30's one-rendering test, and 9.24 writes both shapes for one expression inside a single verse. Heads sit consistently on the content-bearing morpheme under rule 23 - mul, qereb, ayin, mah - but on the governing morpheme where the second adds nothing, as in ka'asher and acharei asher.

Pronoun agreement: 9.7's be-qirbi rendered 'among us' and 9.16's elav rendered 'their' both give a singular suffix a plural English pronoun following the ASV's referent, which rule 18 licenses in the same terms in both places. The waw plus attah pairs (9.6, 9.11, 9.19, 9.23, 9.25) are likewise consistent: attah always takes 'now' and the waw takes whatever connective the ASV wrote, in either English order.

BSB: 25 disagreements, all documented convention differences - articles left unrepresented under rules 29/41/47 (11), object markers under rule 16 (4), prepositions silenced by recasting under rules 40/52 (6), 9.4's waw for which the ASV writes no connective, 9.12's resumptive object suffix under rule 22, 9.25's non-repeated ka under rule 22, and 9.27's ba under rule 40. None is a genuine error and none would justify moving an accepted edge.

9.14's et rendered 'at' is the chapter's only object marker taking English, against thirteen unrepresented; it is rule 16's first family (the English verb reaches its marked object through a preposition, 'asked counsel at the mouth of Jehovah') and is correctly distinguished from the rest.
